932.title: The Salvation Army
932.hook: William and Catherine Booth take soup, soap and salvation into the streets of London's East End
932.howItsDone: Salvation Army corps hold Sunday worship with brass bands and run food banks, shelters and recovery programs, and its officers serve as both ministers and social workers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Spurgeon, who told his students the truth about his own dark days. Your line was even preachers get low. Who did you ask, and really wait for the answer? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

A drum, then a cornet, then a few voices singing, off key and loud, on a street corner in the East End of London. Outside a pub. People stop, some to listen, some to jeer. The singers wear uniforms. Their leader is called the General. If it sounds like the army, that's the point. This is a church that decided to march into the poor streets instead of waiting for the poor to come to church. It was started by a preacher named William Booth and his wife, Catherine, a preacher too. Today, a church with brass bands, ranks, and a pot of soup on the stove.

First, the name. The Booths' work began as the Christian Mission. The story goes that a report described it as a volunteer army, and William crossed out volunteer and wrote salvation. However it happened, the name stuck, and so did the ranks and the uniforms. Second, Catherine. She didn't stand behind her husband. She preached to crowds herself, and she wrote in defense of women preaching, at a time when women in the pulpit were hotly argued over. The Army gave women real leadership from its early days. Third, the order of things. The Army became known by a short phrase: soup, soap, salvation. Feed people. Help them get clean, find a bed, find work. And tell them about the love of God. The phrase puts soup first, and that matters. Hungry people can't hear much. The Booths could point to Isaiah, where God describes the fast he wants, in the King James Bible: "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?" Fourth, what kind of church it is. The Salvation Army is a church in its own right, with its own officers who serve as its ministers. Salvationists don't hold baptism or communion services. They say the inner grace those rites point to is what counts, and they live it out in service. Catholic and Orthodox churches, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans and Anglicans, hold those rites at the very center of their life. Both sides say so openly, and the Army works alongside other churches. And the word salvation itself? In the Greek of the New Testament, it can mean rescue, safety and health, not only heaven. Soup, soap and salvation are three parts of one rescue.

Here's the practice: give soup or soap. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the nearest place that feeds or shelters people near you: a food bank, a shelter, a church pantry, a box by the supermarket door. Then picture your own kitchen or bathroom shelf. Is there a can of soup, a bar of soap, a toothbrush still in its packet? Choose one thing. Set it aside, in your mind now and with your hands later, to give this week. While the bell rings, hold in mind the person who will open it. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
The Salvation Army. A church founded by William and Catherine Booth, with uniforms, brass bands and a mission to the poor streets.
Your line: soup, soap, salvation. Today, before you offer anyone advice or comfort, check whether they need something simpler first: food, water, a seat. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Hudson Taylor
933.hook: an English missionary in China puts on Chinese clothes, grows the braid, and learns the dialects
933.howItsDone: Some Christian mission agencies today ask workers to learn the local language and culture deeply before anything else, and churches in China are led by Chinese Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salvation Army, with its brass bands, its uniforms and its pot of soup. Your line was soup, soap, salvation. Who needed something simple from you first? Day nine hundred thirty-three.

A barber's razor scrapes across the front of a young Englishman's head. The hair at the back is left to grow, so it can be braided into a long queue, the way Chinese men wore it then. He folds away his European suit and puts on the loose robe and cloth shoes of a Chinese teacher. Other foreigners in the port city laugh at him. Some missionaries are embarrassed for him. A few are angry: he's letting the side down. His name is Hudson Taylor, and he has decided that if he's going to live among the people of China, he's going to stop looking like a visitor. Today, a change of clothes that was really a change of direction.

The first change was the map. Taylor wanted to go beyond the port cities on the coast, inland, to the provinces far from the sea. So he founded a mission with the word inland in its name, the China Inland Mission, and he asked the people who joined it to dress as he did, to learn the local dialects, and to live simply among their neighbors. Then the reason he gave. Paul, in the King James Bible, writes: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Taylor applied it to his wardrobe. If a foreign suit was a wall, he would take it off. Then the deeper root. Christians say God did this first. John's Gospel says: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Christian belief, God didn't shout from a distance; he came close, in a body, in a language, in a place. Some readers see his clothes and dialects as a small echo of that. Then the harder part, which picks up the thread of day nine hundred seventeen, on missions and empire. Taylor came to China in an age of empire, when Western powers had used force to open China's ports, and opium was part of that trade. Taylor spoke out against the opium trade, and he wanted the gospel to look Chinese rather than British. But he was still a foreigner, and the clothes didn't change that. In time, Chinese Christians led their own churches, and they hold a range of views about the missionary era. The idea Taylor reached for was simple and costly: don't ask people to become like you. Become one of them, as far as love can take you.
screen: `STILL A FOREIGNER IN AN EMPIRE AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor another culture's ways. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone near you whose culture isn't yours: a neighbor, a coworker, the family who runs the corner shop, a classmate's parents. Think about what you actually know of their ways. A greeting. A holiday. A food. A way of showing respect. Notice how little, or how much. Choose one thing to learn properly this week, by asking them, kindly and with real interest. Not to wear it like a costume. To meet them where they are. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Hudson Taylor. An English missionary who put on Chinese clothes, learned the dialects and went inland, beyond the port cities.
Your line: become one of them. Today, in one conversation, learn the other person's way of doing something before you explain your own. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: Amy Carmichael
934.hook: in south India, a missionary opens her home to girls at risk of exploitation and writes of love that costs
934.howItsDone: Amy Carmichael's books are read for devotion by some Christians, and the household she founded at Dohnavur continues as a community led by Indian Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hudson Taylor, who folded away his suit and went inland. Your line was become one of them. What did you learn about someone else's way? Day nine hundred thirty-four.

Early one morning, a little girl stands at the door of a mission house in south India. She has run away in the night. The story told about her, and told by the woman who opened the door, is that she had been given to a temple as a small child, and she was afraid of what was coming. Her name, in that story, is Preena. The woman at the door is Amy Carmichael, a missionary from Ireland who wears a sari and works alongside Indian women. She takes the child in. The people who claim the girl come to get her back. Amy doesn't hand her over. Today, a home that began with one child.

Through that child and others, Carmichael learned of a custom in parts of India by which some girls were given to temples as children, and some were sexually exploited as they grew. She wasn't the only one to oppose it. Indian reformers, Hindu and Christian, campaigned against the practice too, and Indian law later banned it. Carmichael's part was a home. Over the years it grew into a large household at a place called Dohnavur, later including boys as well. The children called her Amma, mother. Indian coworkers ran much of it beside her. She wanted it to be a family, not an institution. That home had a price. Taking children in made her enemies and brought her trouble. She gave up comfort, home leave, and a life anyone in Ireland would have recognized. In her poems and books she wrote about love that costs: love that gives up nothing, she said, isn't really love. The first letter of John says something close to it, in the King James Bible: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." Deed and truth. Love you can see by what it gives up. Looking back, some Christians remember her with deep gratitude, and some also ask hard questions today about the mission era she worked in. Neither view takes away the girl at the door, or the door that stayed open.

Here's the practice: protect a child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student. Picture their face. Ask one quiet question: is there one thing I could do to make this child safer, or to be an adult they could tell if something were wrong? Maybe it's paying closer attention. Maybe it's a conversation. Maybe it's simply being someone steady. If you're ever worried a child is in danger, the protecting step is to call the people whose job it is. If you pray, you can hold that child before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Amy Carmichael. A missionary in south India who opened her home to girls at risk, and became Amma to a household of children.
Your line: love that costs. Today, do one kind thing that actually costs you something, time, comfort or pride, and don't mention it. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: Bernadette
935.hook: Catholics tell of a poor, sickly girl at Lourdes to whom Mary appeared, and of a spring the sick still come to
935.howItsDone: Catholic pilgrims travel to Lourdes to pray at the grotto, join candlelight processions and bathe in the spring water, and the sick are brought there with volunteers who help care for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amy Carmichael, and a girl at the door who wasn't handed back. Your line was love that costs. What did your kindness cost you? Day nine hundred thirty-five.

Cold water, a riverbank, a girl gathering firewood and bones to sell. That's how the story begins, as Catholics tell it. Her name is Bernadette Soubirous. Her family is poor enough to be living in a former jail cell in the town of Lourdes, in the south of France. She is small, often sick, and can barely read. Near a rocky hollow by the river, a grotto, she says she sees a lady dressed in white, with a rosary. Nobody else sees anything. Her mother is worried. The town is curious. The police are suspicious. Bernadette keeps going back. Today, a girl nobody expected, and a spring in the mud.
screen: `A LADY IN WHITE IN THE GROTTO.`

segments.voice: The spring comes first. In Bernadette's account, the lady told her to drink from the spring and wash in it. There was no spring she could see. So she dug in the muddy ground with her hands, and the crowd watching thought she had lost her mind. Then water began to flow, and it still flows. Then the name. For a long time the lady didn't say who she was. When Bernadette finally asked, she reported the answer in her own local dialect: I am the Immaculate Conception. Bernadette said she didn't know what the words meant, and repeated them all the way to the priest so she wouldn't forget them. In Catholic teaching, the Immaculate Conception means that Mary was kept free from original sin from the moment her life began. Then, who says what, because the churches differ here. The Catholic Church investigated, and judged that the appearances could be believed. It also teaches that no Catholic is required to believe in private revelations like this one. Orthodox Christians honor Mary deeply, but describe her holiness in their own terms. Protestant churches don't treat visions like this as part of their teaching. And Bernadette herself? She didn't stay to be famous. She became a nun, far from Lourdes, often ill, and the Catholic Church later named her a saint. And the spring? The sick are brought there to pray and to bathe, and the Church examines claims of healing carefully. Christians in other churches pray for the sick too, wherever they are, as the letter of James describes, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him."

Here's the practice: pray for the sick. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick right now. Someone in hospital, someone at home with something that won't lift, someone whose illness nobody can see. Picture them as clearly as you can, not their illness, them. Then add one more: someone sick whom nobody is praying for, a stranger in a ward somewhere. If you pray, you can hold them both before God, or, if it's your way, ask Mary to pray for them. If you don't pray, simply wish them strength, and think of one thing you could do for the first person this week. The bell holds the time.
Bernadette. A poor, sickly girl from Lourdes who said Mary appeared to her at a grotto, and who dug in the mud until water came.

Your line: the spring at the grotto. Today, when you meet someone who is unwell or worn down, do one plain thing for them, a call, an errand, a meal, without waiting to be asked. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: The little way
936.hook: Thérèse of Lisieux finds holiness in small things done with great love
936.howItsDone: Catholics keep Thérèse's feast day and read Story of a Soul, and some Christians take up her little way by offering ordinary tasks and small kindnesses to God through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette, digging in the mud at Lourdes until water came. Your line was the spring at the grotto. Who did you offer something simple to? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

Dirty water keeps landing on a young nun's face. She's at the laundry tubs in a convent in Lisieux, in France, and the sister working beside her is scrubbing so hard that the spray flies every time. The young nun wants to step back and wipe her face. She wants, maybe, to say something. Instead, she decides to stand there and take it as a small gift. She tells this story herself, in her memoir. It's not a dramatic story. That's the point. Her name is Thérèse, and she spent the rest of her short life inside those convent walls, finding a way to God made entirely of moments like this. Today, the little way.

Thérèse read about the great saints and felt like a grain of sand next to a mountain. In her memoir, later published as Story of a Soul, she says she was too small to climb the steep stairway of perfection. So she went looking for another way up. She lived in a time of new inventions, and she pictured an elevator: something that carries you up when you can't climb. She found it in two lines of scripture. Proverbs, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." And Isaiah: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you." The lift, she decided, was being carried. Not climbing harder, but staying small and letting God's arms do the lifting. Jesus says something close in Matthew, in the King James Bible: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." In a day, it looked like this. Not great deeds. A smile for a sister who got on her nerves. Not answering back. Letting the water hit her face. Doing the dull job carefully. She described these as flowers she could scatter, small things no one would notice, done with as much love as she could put into them. Thérèse died young, inside the same convent. The Catholic Church later named her a saint, and a Doctor of the Church, a title for teachers whose writing is trusted to guide the whole Church. Christians outside the Catholic Church read her book too, and what they find in it is laundry tubs, chores and small kindnesses.

Here's the practice: do one small thing with great love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind your day, and look for the smallest, dullest job in it. Folding laundry. A reply to an email. Making a bed. Listening to someone tell a story you've heard before. Pick one. Now picture doing it slowly and carefully, as if it were for someone you love, because maybe it is. Notice whether anyone will see it. Probably not. That's fine. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you start, the way Thérèse did. The bell holds the time.
The little way. Thérèse of Lisieux's path to God through small, hidden things done with love, trusting God like a child.
Your line: small things, great love. Today, do the job you'd normally rush with care, and let nobody know you meant it. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Damien of Molokai
937.hook: a priest goes to a settlement for people with leprosy, and one day begins his sermon, we lepers
937.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Damien's feast and pray for people with Hansen's disease and for those who care for them, and Christians of other churches also tell his story when they talk about serving people pushed to the margins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse of Lisieux and the little way. Your line was small things, great love. Which small thing did you do with care, and did anyone notice? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

Boats struggle to land at this beach. The cliffs behind it are a wall, and the sea in front is rough, so people are put ashore however the crew can manage. Once they're here, they don't leave. This strip of land on the Hawaiian island of Molokai is where the kingdom sent people with leprosy, the disease now called Hansen's disease, to keep them away from everyone else. Families said goodbye on the dock in Honolulu. A young Belgian priest, Father Damien, offers to go. He builds houses, digs graves, dresses sores, plays with the children. And one Sunday, tradition says, he stands up to preach and changes a single word. Today, that word.

Damien had preached to the settlement the way an outsider would. You. Your suffering. Your hope. Then he noticed the signs of the disease on his own body. He had caught it. The story told about the next Sunday is short: he began his sermon with two words, we lepers. Not you. We. Hold that word for a moment, because it's the whole lesson. Plenty of people did good things for the settlement from a safe distance. Damien was now inside the thing he'd come to help with, with no way back out. And the people he served, the story goes, heard the difference. There's a scene in the Gospel of Mark behind all of this. A man with leprosy kneels in front of Jesus and says, if you want to, you can make me clean. In the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him." Touched him. The law of the time kept people with that disease apart, and the story stops to say that Jesus reached out a hand before he said a word. The Letter to the Hebrews says something close about Jesus and the people he came for: "he is not ashamed to call them brethren." Some Christians have read Damien's life as that sentence, lived out on a beach. He kept working after the diagnosis, and the disease took his life on Molokai. The Catholic Church names him a saint, and Christians of other churches honor him too. One more honest note. Some of the people sent to Molokai would rather not be called lepers at all. It names a person by a disease. Damien could say the word only because he'd become one of them. Today's lesson isn't the label. It's the we.

Here's the practice: stand with an outcast, starting in your head. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a group people talk about as they. The unhoused man on the corner. The kid nobody sits with. People with an illness others are afraid of. Notice how your mind describes them. Then, quietly, try the word we. We who get sick. We who get left out. We who need a hand. Don't force a feeling. Just try the grammar. If you pray, you can pray for them as we instead of they. If you don't, let the we sit there. The bell holds the time.
Damien of Molokai. A priest who went to live with people the world had sent away, caught their disease, and began to preach as one of them.
Your line: we lepers. Today, the next time you hear yourself say they about people pushed to the edge, try saying we, out loud or in your head, and see what changes. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: Charles de Foucauld
938.hook: a soldier turned hermit lives among the Tuareg in the Sahara as a brother to all
938.howItsDone: Small communities of laypeople, priests and religious sisters inspired by Charles de Foucauld live simply among poor neighbors, working ordinary jobs and keeping a time of quiet prayer each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damien of Molokai, the priest who caught the disease and began his sermon, we lepers. Did you try saying we about someone you usually call they? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

A young French cavalry officer throws parties, runs up debts, and gets disciplined for bringing a mistress along on a posting to North Africa. Faith means nothing to him. Years later the same man is living in a small hut deep in the Sahara, with a notebook of words in the language of the Tuareg, the desert people around him, and a chapel the size of a closet. Nobody from his old life would recognize him. He doesn't preach on street corners. He doesn't run a school. Mostly, he's just there, with his door open. What he wanted to be called is today's line.

Charles de Foucauld came back to faith as a young man, and he went looking for the plainest life he could find. He tried a monastery, and left it for something even smaller. What drew him was a part of Jesus's life the Gospels barely describe: the long quiet years in Nazareth. Luke gives it barely two verses. In the King James Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them." No sermons, no miracles, just a carpenter's household. Foucauld decided that hidden life was a way to follow Jesus too. So he went deep into the desert and set out to be a neighbor. He learned the Tuareg language well enough to gather their poems and write down their words. He gave out medicine and grain, and sat with whoever came by. He wrote that he wanted the people around him, Christian, Muslim, Jewish or anyone else, to look on him as a brother, a universal brother, and he called his little house the fraternity. In Luke, a lawyer asks Jesus who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stops for a beaten stranger, then turns the question around, in the King James Bible: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Some readers hear Foucauld's life as an answer. He did not build a large church. He died at his own door during a raid in the desert. But others later formed communities inspired by him, small groups who live and work among the poor, and the Catholic Church has named him a saint. Look back at this week. Soup, soap and salvation in the East End. Hudson Taylor in Chinese clothes, becoming one of them. Amy Carmichael's love that costs. The spring at the grotto. Small things, great love. We lepers. And now a man in the desert who wanted only to be a brother. Seven stories, one direction: closer.

Here's the practice: be a brother, or a sister, to someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person near you who isn't family and isn't quite a friend. A coworker. A neighbor. The person who cleans your building. Notice what you know about them. Maybe only a name. Maybe not even that. Foucauld's whole method was attention: a language learned, a door open, time given. Choose one small brotherly thing you could do for that person this week. Learn their name. Ask how they are and wait for the answer. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Charles de Foucauld. A soldier who became a hermit in the Sahara and hoped everyone around him would call him brother.
Your line: universal brother. Today, treat one person outside your usual circle as family for a minute: a name used, a question asked, a door held open. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.
